🚨 A regulatory filing can be used as camouflage

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has charged 38 entities, alleging that they submitted false information in Forms ADV to appear legitimate to American investors.

According to the SEC, the filings included:

• business addresses where the firms had no physical presence
• disconnected phone numbers or numbers belonging to unrelated companies
• nearly identical ownership structures and financial data
• claims involving audit firms that could not be found in public registries

Some of the entities were also promoted through websites displaying fake certificates claiming that they were registered with the SEC.

The charges are allegations, but the case demonstrates an important security lesson:

Finding a company in a regulatory database is only the beginning of verification.

The legal name, registration status, contact details, permissions and people behind the business must all match.

A professional-looking filing can create credibility.

It cannot replace independent verification.

🪖☪️Mecca’s New Defense Brand

Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan held the first meeting of their new security committee in Istanbul. Foreign ministers, defense ministers and military chiefs attended. Hakan Fidan announced the formal name: the Mecca Defense Alliance.

Fidan said the pact is defensive, not directed at any country and does not replace Turkey’s NATO obligations. He also said it is open to regional states that support “peace and stability.” Egypt may join, he said, but Ankara is still drafting entry conditions and procedures.

The structure is already becoming real. Pakistan will provide the alliance’s first secretary-general for three years. The permanent secretariat will be based in Saudi Arabia. The members plan joint exercises, defense-industry cooperation, technology development and joint production. “Not directed against anyone” is how every new alliance introduces itself before it starts ordering maps.

Then Fidan supplied the target that does not officially exist. He called Benjamin Netanyahu a threat to “global security” and linked harsher Israeli rhetoric toward Turkey to Israel’s coming election. Ankara says Mecca targets nobody. Its foreign minister then spent the press conference describing one man as a danger to humanity.

The pact’s Article 5-style pledge says an attack on one signatory will be treated as an attack on all. It was signed against the backdrop of the Iran war, attacks in the Gulf, and rising tension between Israel and Turkey in Syria. Saudi Arabia brings money and religious legitimacy. Pakistan brings a nuclear deterrent. Turkey brings NATO membership, an army and the regional sales team.

The alliance says it will reduce uncertainty. It has already added one certainty. The Middle East is building another security structure without waiting for Washington’s approval.

Avocado Cheddar Cheese 🧀 Crackers: 

Ingredients
2 cups all-purpose flour
1/2 teaspoon baking powder
1 1/4 cups ripe avocado (mashed or blended smooth)
4 tablespoons melted butter
1/2 cup grated cheddar cheese (mild cheddar works well)
Salt to taste

Instructions:
Preheat your oven to 375°F (190°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Combine the ingredients in a blender or food processor, mixing the ripe avocado, grated cheese, flour, baking powder, salt, and melted butter until a smooth dough forms.

Roll out the dough onto the parchment-lined baking sheet until it is about 1/2 inch thick or thinner for crispier crackers. 

Score or cut the dough into small cracker squares.

Bake at 375°F for about 15 minutes, or until they turn lightly browned and crisp.

🧈 The Extra Butter Coating
2 tablespoons melted butter
1 teaspoon garlic powder
Optional: A pinch of Italian seasoning or sea salt 

Simply whisk the garlic powder and herbs into the melted butter, pour it over your baked crackers, and gently toss them in a bowl until they are completely coated. It gives them an amazing garlic-butter crust that pairs perfectly with the cheddar and avocado!

Cool the crackers completely, then store them in an airtight container for 4 to 5 days. Freeze afterwards if long term storage is needed.

Ceuta’s Blame Budget

Pedro Sánchez has found a way to discuss a border crisis without discussing the border. Spain will spend €168 million to revive Ceuta’s economy after at least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco in late July. 

The sum equals about 8% of the enclave’s GDP and comes on top of €180 million pledged earlier for medium-term recovery.

Sánchez says the European Union’s foreign service found signs that Russian and Israeli networks spread and amplified false claims about Spain’s migration rules. 

One rumor said anyone who reached Ceuta by swimming could not be returned to Morocco. Sánchez also blamed an international far-right network for turning the migration surge into an attack on Spain and Europe.

The evidence cited publicly is about online amplification, not proof that Russia or Israel organized the crossing. 

Sánchez said he saw no evidence that Moroccan authorities were involved. That is politically convenient. Morocco controls the border. Russia and Israel control the algorithm, apparently.

Italy has extended its temporary checks on air and sea arrivals from Spain for another 15 days. Spain has answered with matching controls for arrivals from Italy. 

Europe’s open-border system is now getting a bilateral stress test because one Spanish enclave sits on the African coast.

Sánchez promises cooperation with Morocco. Italy promises inspections. The EU promises an investigation. 

And Ceuta gets €168 million to recover from a crisis whose authors, according to Madrid, live somewhere between Rabat, Moscow, Tel Aviv and the comment section.
